notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Generate a uniform integer from 1 through 10 using only a uniform rand7 source.
Idea: Draw two rand7 values to form x=(rand7()-1)*7+rand7(), covering 1..49 uniformly; reject x>40 and map accepted values with (x-1)%10+1.
Technique and why it applies: Rejection sampling discards the nine excess outcomes so each of the ten returned residues has four equally likely accepted inputs.
Invariant: Each accepted x maps to exactly one value in 1..10, and every result has the same number of preimages among accepted values.
Edge cases: The first possible draw maps to 1; x=40 maps to 10; x=41 is rejected and the loop retries. Expected work is finite but the loop has no fixed iteration bound.
Complexity: O(1) expected time per result and O(1) extra space, because each attempt draws two values and succeeds with probability 40/49.
complexity_reason: Each attempt calls rand7 twice, rejects 9 of the 49 equally likely pairs, and stores only x.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Implement uniform rand10 using only the uniform rand7 method inherited from SolBase.
Idea: Combine two draws into x in 1..49, repeat while x>40, and map each accepted value to (x-1)%10+1.
Technique and why it applies: Rejection sampling removes the nine outcomes that cannot be evenly divided among ten results.
Invariant: Each result from 1 through 10 corresponds to four accepted x values, so accepted outcomes have equal probability.
Edge cases: Accepted x=1 returns 1 and x=40 returns 10; x=49 is rejected. The while loop may retry any number of times, but succeeds with probability 40/49 per attempt.
Complexity: O(1) expected time and O(1) auxiliary space, since each attempt uses two rand7 calls and a few integer variables.
complexity_reason: Each iteration combines two uniform draws and accepts 40 of 49 possible values, retaining only one integer.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Determine whether all positive matchstick lengths can form four equal sides without cutting any stick.
Idea: Reject totals not divisible by four; sort sticks descending, reject a largest stick above target, then DFS assigns each stick to a side without exceeding target.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking explores side assignments while descending sort and duplicate-side pruning reduce equivalent choices.
Invariant: At recursion depth i, the first i sticks have been assigned without any side exceeding target.
Edge cases: A total not divisible by four returns false; a stick longer than target is impossible to place; equal current side sums are tried only once. The input list is sorted in place.
Complexity: Worst-case exponential time in the number of sticks, with O(n) recursion depth plus four side totals and a small seen set.
complexity_reason: The DFS may branch over four side choices per stick, while recursion depth grows with the number of matchsticks.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Check whether every matchstick can be assigned intact to one of four sides of equal length.
Idea: Sum lengths and reject non-divisible totals; clone and sort sticks descending, then recursively add each stick to a side only if its sum stays within target.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking searches assignments and prunes branches that exceed target or repeat a side sum.
Invariant: At dfs(i), exactly the first i sorted sticks have been placed, and each side total is at most target.
Edge cases: A total not divisible by four fails immediately; a largest stick above target cannot fit; equal side totals are skipped. The clone preserves the caller's array order, while int total assumes problem constraints prevent overflow.
Complexity: Worst-case exponential time with O(n) recursion depth and a set of at most four side totals per call.
complexity_reason: The recursive search may try four side placements for each stick, and its call stack grows with n.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Choose the largest subset of binary strings using at most m zeros and n ones.
Idea: For each string count zeros and ones, then update dp[i][j] in descending resource order with max(current, 1+dp[i-zeros][j-ones]).
Technique and why it applies: Two-resource 0/1 knapsack treats each string as one item with a zero cost and a one cost.
Invariant: Descending loops ensure the current string cannot be reused multiple times during its own DP update.
Edge cases: An empty string costs no zeros or ones and can increment the selected count once; budgets smaller than a string's counts skip it; descending order prevents repeated use. The inputs are assumed binary strings.
Complexity: O(L + S*m*n) time and O(m*n) space, where S is string count and L is total characters counted.
complexity_reason: Each string is counted once and updates at most (m+1)(n+1) DP states stored in a fixed two-dimensional table.

notes:
Task and constraints: Choose the largest subset of binary strings in strs while using at most m zeros and n ones.
Idea: For each s in strs, count z by scanning its characters and set o=s.length()-z; then update dp[i][j] in descending budget order using 1+dp[i-z][j-o].
Technique and why it applies: Two-resource 0/1 knapsack tracks the best subset size for each zero/one budget pair, treating each string as one item.
Invariant: After each processed string, dp[i][j] is the largest subset count achievable from the processed prefix using no more than i zeros and j ones.
Edge cases: A string containing only zeros consumes no one budget; if z>m or o>n it cannot update dp[m][n]; descending i and j prevent reusing the current s twice. The method assumes strs contains binary strings.
Complexity: O(L + S*m*n) time and O(m*n) space, where L is total string length and S is the number of strings.
complexity_reason: The code scans each s to count z and o, then visits the feasible dp[i][j] states in descending order for every string.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Find the smallest radius so each house position is covered by at least one heater.
Idea: Sort heaters; for each house use bisect_left to find the first heater at or right of it, compute distances to that heater and its predecessor, and maximize the nearer distance.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search identifies the two only heater candidates that can be nearest to a house in sorted order.
Invariant: answer is the maximum, over houses, of each house's distance to its nearest heater.
Edge cases: A house before all heaters uses only the right candidate; a house after all heaters uses only the left; an exact heater match gives distance zero. At least one heater is assumed, and sorting mutates heaters.
Complexity: O(h log h + n log h) time and O(1) extra space beyond sorting, for h heaters and n houses.
complexity_reason: The heaters are sorted once and each of n houses performs one binary search plus constant distance calculations.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Return the minimum coverage radius needed for all houses given heater positions.
Idea: Sort heaters, binary-search each house with Arrays.binarySearch, convert a negative result to insertion point, compare adjacent distances, and maximize the minimum.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search finds the nearest heater candidates around each house without scanning all heaters.
Invariant: For each house, the nearer of the insertion-point neighbors gives the least radius needed to cover that house.
Edge cases: A house exactly at a heater has distance zero; houses beyond either end use the one available neighbor; the problem assumes at least one heater. Long distances prevent subtraction overflow, and the result is cast to int under problem bounds.
Complexity: O(h log h + n log h) time and O(1) explicit extra space beyond sorting, for h heaters and n houses.
complexity_reason: Sorting costs O(h log h), and each house uses one binary search and a constant number of distance comparisons.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Return the bitwise complement of a positive integer using only its significant binary positions.
Idea: Create mask=(1<<num.bit_length())-1, which has one bits through num's highest set bit, then XOR num with that mask.
Technique and why it applies: A width-limited all-ones mask flips only significant bits and avoids Python's unbounded signed complement behavior.
Invariant: mask has exactly as many low one bits as num has binary digits, so XOR changes those positions and no higher ones.
Edge cases: num=1 returns 0; num=5 (101) returns 2 (010); zero is excluded because its bit length would produce a zero mask.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space under fixed-width integer constraints; bit_length and XOR operate on the integer representation.
complexity_reason: The method computes one bit-length mask and performs one XOR without iterating over input-sized structures.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Complement a positive integer only within the width of its significant binary representation.
Idea: Start mask at one and left-shift until it exceeds num; mask-1 then has ones at all significant positions, and XOR returns the complement.
Technique and why it applies: A generated bit mask limits flipping to the number's actual binary width instead of sign-extending the complement.
Invariant: At loop exit mask is the first power of two greater than num, so mask-1 contains ones exactly through num's highest set bit.
Edge cases: num=1 returns 0; num=5 returns 2; positive input is assumed. The loop uses int shifts and relies on the problem's upper bound staying below overflow of the mask.
Complexity: O(log num) time and O(1) extra space because mask doubles on each iteration and no collection is allocated.
complexity_reason: The while loop doubles mask until it exceeds num, requiring logarithmically many shifts and constant storage.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Sum Hamming distances over all unordered pairs of integers in nums.
Idea: For each of 32 bit positions count ones, then add ones*(n-ones), the number of pairs that disagree at that position.
Technique and why it applies: Bitwise counting decomposes pair distances by position, counting every differing pair once per bit.
Invariant: At a fixed bit, every pair with one set bit and one clear bit contributes exactly one, and no other pair contributes.
Edge cases: An empty or singleton array returns zero; identical values contribute no differing positions; the loop checks all 32 positions of the expected integer range.
Complexity: O(32n), effectively O(n), time and O(1) extra space because each bit scans nums and keeps a counter.
complexity_reason: The code scans all n values for each of 32 bit positions and stores only counts and the total.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Compute the sum of Hamming distances for every pair in an int array.
Idea: For each bit b from 0 through 31, count set bits using unsigned shift, then add ones*(n-ones) to long total.
Technique and why it applies: Counting zeros-versus-ones pairs at each bit avoids comparing every pair directly.
Invariant: At each bit position, exactly ones*(n-ones) unordered pairs differ, so summing positions gives total pair distance.
Edge cases: Empty or singleton arrays return zero; equal numbers contribute zero; >>> treats negative int bit patterns as unsigned for shifting. The final int cast assumes the answer fits the problem's range.
Complexity: O(32n), effectively O(n), time and O(1) extra space because each bit scans the array with scalar counters.
complexity_reason: The inner loop reads n integers for each of 32 bit positions and retains only the count and long total.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Generate a random point uniformly by area inside or on a circle of radius r centered at (x,y).
Idea: Choose a uniform angle theta and radius r*sqrt(U), then offset the center by the cosine and sine components.
Technique and why it applies: Uniform angle plus square-root-scaled radius compensates for the increasing area of outer rings.
Invariant: The sampled angle covers directions uniformly, while the squared normalized radius is uniform from zero to one, making equal-area disks equally likely.
Edge cases: Radius zero always returns the center; U near zero yields a point near the center; theta spans a full revolution. Floating-point output is approximate.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) extra space because each call draws two random values and computes two coordinates.
complexity_reason: Each call draws two random numbers, evaluates fixed trigonometric operations, and returns a two-value list.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Sample a point uniformly by area inside a circle with a fixed radius and center.
Idea: Draw theta uniformly from 0 to 2π and radius*sqrt(U), then return center plus the radius-scaled cosine and sine coordinates.
Technique and why it applies: The square-root radial transform corrects for the fact that a ring's area grows with its radius.
Invariant: The angle is uniform and the squared distance from the center is uniform over the disk's normalized area.
Edge cases: Zero radius always returns the center; the angle covers a complete revolution; floating-point results are approximate. Random's nextDouble supplies values in [0,1), so the boundary is approached rather than guaranteed.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) extra space per point because the method performs a fixed number of random and math operations.
complexity_reason: The method draws two doubles, computes fixed trigonometric expressions, and allocates one two-element result array.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Format a license key into uppercase groups of length k separated by dashes, allowing a shorter first group.
Idea: Remove dashes and uppercase the remaining characters; compute len(clean)%k for the first group, slice the rest into k-sized groups, and join with dashes.
Technique and why it applies: String slicing groups the cleaned key from the left after determining the only possible short prefix.
Invariant: Every group after the optional first group has length k, and concatenation preserves all non-dash characters in uppercase.
Edge cases: An input containing only dashes returns an empty string; a clean length divisible by k has no short first group; lowercase letters are uppercased. k must be positive.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for cleaning, slicing groups, and joining the formatted result.
complexity_reason: The code scans s to clean it, slices the cleaned string into groups, and constructs a result of linear length.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Format an alphanumeric key into uppercase groups of k characters, separated by dashes, with a possibly shorter first group.
Idea: Remove dashes and uppercase with Locale.ROOT; scan the cleaned string right to left, inserting a dash after each k emitted characters, then reverse the builder.
Technique and why it applies: Building groups from the right naturally creates full groups first and leaves the first group shorter when needed.
Invariant: Before reversal, out contains the processed suffix in reverse character order with separators inserted after each group of k.
Edge cases: Only dashes produces an empty string; a length divisible by k has no short leading group; Locale.ROOT avoids locale-dependent casing. k must be positive.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for the cleaned string and StringBuilder, since each character is scanned and reversed once.
complexity_reason: The method creates a cleaned string, traverses its characters once, and reverses a builder proportional to input length.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Return the maximum length of a consecutive run of ones in a binary array.
Idea: Increase curr when x is 1 and update best; reset curr to zero on any other value.
Technique and why it applies: A running streak count tracks only the current contiguous run, while best preserves the longest run already seen.
Invariant: curr equals the length of the trailing run of ones in the processed prefix, and best is its maximum over that prefix.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; [1,1,1] returns three; a zero resets the current run. The code treats values other than exactly 1 as separators.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space because each element updates two counters once.
complexity_reason: The loop reads each array element once and maintains only curr and best.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Find the largest consecutive sequence of ones in an int array.
Idea: For each x, increment curr and maximize best when x==1; otherwise reset curr to zero.
Technique and why it applies: A single-pass streak counter records contiguous ones without storing their positions.
Invariant: curr measures the suffix of ones ending at the current index, while best records the largest suffix length encountered.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; [1,1,1] returns three; any non-one value resets the run. Only primitive counters are used, and the method returns zero for no elements.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, since each array entry is checked once and two counters are retained.
complexity_reason: The enhanced loop visits each integer once and uses constant-time comparisons and updates.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Decide whether the first player can secure at least the second player's score when each move takes the left or right end.
Idea: Initialize dp with nums; for increasing interval lengths, replace dp[i] with the better score difference from taking nums[i] or nums[j], then return dp[0]>=0.
Technique and why it applies: Interval dynamic programming stores the best score difference the current player can force on each subarray.
Invariant: When processing length L, dp[i] and dp[i+1] represent the optimal differences for shorter intervals needed to evaluate nums[i:j+1].
Edge cases: A singleton has a nonnegative score difference; equal totals can return true; the standard constraints require a nonempty array because dp[0] is read. Python integers handle score arithmetic.
Complexity: O(n²) time and O(n) extra space, as all interval lengths and starts are evaluated while dp stores one value per start index.
complexity_reason: The nested loops evaluate O(n²) intervals and reuse a one-dimensional dp array of n values.

notes:
Task and constraints: Task and constraints: Determine whether player one can obtain a score at least equal to player two when players take either end of the remaining array.
Idea: Clone nums into dp; for each interval length, update dp[i] with max(nums[i]-dp[i+1], nums[j]-dp[i]), then check whether dp[0] is nonnegative.
Technique and why it applies: Interval DP evaluates optimal score difference from either end and compresses all interval states into one array.
Invariant: During each length pass, dp[i+1] still holds the previous-length interval value, while dp[i] is replaced with the current interval's best difference.
Edge cases: A single-element array returns true; ties return true because comparison uses >=; empty input would fail at dp[0] and is outside constraints. int arithmetic assumes score differences fit.
Complexity: O(n²) time and O(n) extra space because each interval is processed once and the cloned DP array has n entries.
complexity_reason: The nested length and start loops examine O(n²) intervals, while dp retains n integers.
